subject: film
title: Pre-Code Hollywood, 1929 to 1934
dek: For about four years after sound arrived, American studios made films in which women slept their way to the top floor of a bank, gangsters died in the rain as heroes, a chain-gang convict escaped into the dark with no happy ending, and Mae West joked about sex in nearly every line. A moral code for movies already existed on paper, but almost nobody enforced it. Then, in the summer of 1934, Catholic boycotts and a new office run by Joseph Breen made the code law inside the industry, and it shaped Hollywood for the next thirty-four years. This lesson covers why the code existed, what the pre-Code films did with their freedom, especially for women on screen, how the crackdown happened, and what was happening in Shanghai, Berlin, Tokyo and Taipei at the same time.
era: c. 1929 to 1934: from the coming of sound and the writing of the Production Code to the creation of the Production Code Administration in July 1934, with a look at the years before and after
honesty: This lesson keeps to facts documented in the English Wikipedia articles on pre-Code Hollywood, the Motion Picture Production Code, the films and the people named, in the text of the 1930 Code itself, and in standard histories such as Thomas Doherty's Pre-Code Hollywood (1999). Box-office and attendance figures from the period are estimates, so the lesson avoids exact numbers it could not check. There are no images today rather than risk pictures that do not match their captions.

timeline.label: Films are not free speech
timeline.detail: In Mutual Film Corporation v. Industrial Commission of Ohio, the US Supreme Court rules that films are a business, not speech protected by the First Amendment, so states and cities may censor them.

timeline.label: Will Hays hired
timeline.detail: After a run of Hollywood scandals, including the Roscoe 'Fatty' Arbuckle case, the studios form a trade group, later called the MPPDA, and hire the former Postmaster General Will H. Hays to clean up the industry's image.

timeline.label: Don'ts and Be Carefuls; The Jazz Singer
timeline.detail: The Hays office issues a list of eleven things never to show and twenty-five to handle carefully. In October, The Jazz Singer brings synchronised dialogue and songs into a feature film.

timeline.label: The Production Code adopted
timeline.detail: Written by the Jesuit priest Daniel Lord and the trade publisher Martin Quigley, the Code is adopted by the studios in 1930. Enforcement is left to a small Studio Relations Committee with little power.

timeline.label: Morocco and The Divorcee
timeline.detail: Marlene Dietrich, in a man's tuxedo, kisses a woman in Josef von Sternberg's Morocco. Norma Shearer wins the Academy Award for Best Actress as a wife who answers her husband's affair with her own in The Divorcee.

timeline.label: Gangsters and monsters
timeline.detail: Little Caesar, The Public Enemy, Dracula and Frankenstein are released. Barbara Stanwyck stars in Night Nurse.

timeline.label: Scarface, Freaks, I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang
timeline.detail: Howard Hawks's Scarface reaches cinemas after a long fight with censors; Tod Browning's Freaks shocks audiences; Mervyn LeRoy's chain-gang film ends with its hero living as a hunted man.

timeline.label: Red-Headed Woman
timeline.detail: Jean Harlow plays a secretary who breaks up her boss's marriage in a comedy written by Anita Loos, and is not punished for it.

timeline.label: Baby Face and She Done Him Wrong
timeline.detail: Stanwyck climbs a bank's office building floor by floor in Baby Face. Mae West's She Done Him Wrong becomes a huge hit for Paramount, then in receivership, and is nominated for Best Picture.

timeline.label: Busby Berkeley and the Depression
timeline.detail: 42nd Street and Gold Diggers of 1933 mix chorus-girl spectacle with the Depression; the Payne Fund Studies and the book Our Movie Made Children claim films harm children.

timeline.label: Catholic campaign begins
timeline.detail: In October the Apostolic Delegate Amleto Cicognani calls on American Catholics to fight immoral films. The bishops form the Legion of Decency, and millions of Catholics sign its pledge in 1934.

timeline.label: The Production Code Administration
timeline.detail: In June 1934 the studios agree to a stronger system. From July, the new Production Code Administration under Joseph Breen must approve every film, and member companies face a $25,000 fine for releasing a film without its seal.

timeline.label: Shanghai: The Goddess
timeline.detail: Ruan Lingyu plays a mother who sells sex to pay for her son's schooling in Wu Yonggang's silent film The Goddess.

timeline.label: The Code weakens
timeline.detail: Otto Preminger releases The Moon Is Blue (1953) without a seal and it still makes money; Some Like It Hot (1959) is also released without one. The Code is rewritten in 1966.

timeline.label: Ratings replace the Code
timeline.detail: On 1 November 1968 the MPAA replaces the Production Code with a film rating system, the start of the G, M, R and X categories.

timeline.label: Baby Face uncut
timeline.detail: A print of the original, uncensored version of Baby Face is found at the Library of Congress and screened at the London Film Festival.

fun_fact.title: Mae West never said the line everyone quotes
fun_fact.text: The line people remember as 'Come up and see me sometime' is not quite what Mae West says in She Done Him Wrong. On screen she tells Cary Grant, 'Why don't you come up sometime and see me?' The shorter version spread through impressions, newspaper columns and later cartoons, and West herself began using the popular version afterwards because audiences expected it. Her real line is slower and more casual, which is exactly how she wanted it to sound.

sections.title: Scandals, censors and a code nobody enforced

blocks.text: American films were censored long before Hollywood had a code. In 1915 the Supreme Court decided in Mutual Film Corporation v. Industrial Commission of Ohio that films were a business, 'pure and simple', and not speech protected by the First Amendment. That meant states and cities could set up their own censorship boards, and many did. A film might be cut one way in New York, another way in Pennsylvania, and banned in Kansas. For the studios this was expensive and unpredictable.

In the early 1920s a series of scandals made it worse. The comedian Roscoe 'Fatty' Arbuckle was tried three times for manslaughter after a woman died following a party in 1921, and was acquitted, but his career was destroyed; the director William Desmond Taylor was murdered in 1922 and the case was never solved. Newspapers presented Hollywood as a place of drink, drugs and sex. To protect themselves from federal regulation, the studios formed a trade group, the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America (MPPDA), and in 1922 hired Will H. Hays, a Presbyterian elder and former Postmaster General, to run it. The press called it the Hays Office.

Hays's first tools were soft. In 1927 his office issued a list known as the 'Don'ts and Be Carefuls': eleven subjects never to show, such as profanity, nudity and ridicule of the clergy, and twenty-five to handle with care, such as sympathy for criminals and 'excessive or lustful kissing'. In 1929 the Catholic publisher Martin Quigley and the Jesuit priest Daniel Lord drafted a fuller document, the Motion Picture Production Code, and the studios adopted it in 1930. Its general principle was that 'no picture shall be produced that will lower the moral standards of those who see it', and that the sympathy of the audience 'shall never be thrown to the side of crime, wrongdoing, evil or sin.'

The Code had rules about almost everything: adultery could not be shown as attractive, crime had to be punished, ministers could not be comic villains, and 'sex perversion or any inference to it' was forbidden, which meant gay and lesbian characters. It also banned 'miscegenation', meaning romantic relationships between white and Black characters, which tells you that the Code protected racial segregation as well as sexual morals. But in 1930 the Code had no teeth. It was administered by a small Studio Relations Committee, led first by Jason Joy and then James Wingate, which could advise and negotiate but could not stop a studio from releasing a film.

sections.title: Sound, the Depression and a struggle for audiences

blocks.text: Two big changes explain why the films of 1930 to 1934 were so bold. The first was sound. After The Jazz Singer in October 1927, studios rushed to make talking pictures, and dialogue made everything sharper. A silent film could suggest sex with a look; a talkie could make a joke about it, and audiences heard the joke. Writers from Broadway and newspapers came to Hollywood and brought fast, cynical talk with them.

The second change was the Great Depression. After the stock market crash of October 1929, cinema attendance at first held up, then fell sharply in the early 1930s. Paramount went into receivership in 1933, RKO and Fox were in serious trouble, and Warner Bros. lost money. Studios competed for a smaller audience with what sold: sex, crime, violence and stories about people who had lost faith in banks, police and government. Many critics have argued that the films were bold partly because the audience was angry, and the studios gave them heroes who broke rules that seemed to have failed anyway.

items: Fallen women and kept women. Stories about women who use sex to get money, jobs or status, often without being punished at the end.
Gangster films. Little Caesar (1931), The Public Enemy (1931) and Scarface (1932) made criminals into charismatic, modern heroes, even when they died at the end.
Social problem films. Warner Bros. made films about chain gangs, corrupt banks, homeless children and unemployed veterans, taken from the headlines.
Horror. Universal's Dracula and Frankenstein (both 1931) and Paramount's Island of Lost Souls (1932) showed violence and bodily horror that later films could only suggest.
Sophisticated comedy and musicals. Ernst Lubitsch's comedies and Busby Berkeley's dance numbers treated sex as something adult and funny.

sections.title: Complicated women: what pre-Code films let women do

blocks.text: The most interesting thing about pre-Code Hollywood for a feminist history is how many films were about women who wanted money, work and sex, and said so. The critic Mick LaSalle called his 2000 book on the period Complicated Women, and his argument is that the women of 1930 to 1934 were allowed to be ambitious, angry, adulterous and funny in ways that would not return to American films for decades.

Norma Shearer won the Academy Award for Best Actress for The Divorcee (1930). She plays a wife who discovers her husband's affair, and when he says it meant nothing, she has an affair of her own and tells him she has 'balanced their accounts'. The film still ends with a reconciliation, but it treats her anger and her desire as reasonable. In Night Nurse (1931), directed by William Wellman, Barbara Stanwyck and Joan Blondell play nurses who undress in front of the camera, joke with each other, and uncover a plot to starve two children for their inheritance, while the police are useless. In Female (1933), Ruth Chatterton runs a car company and treats her male employees the way male bosses in films treated secretaries.

Baby Face (1933) is the clearest example. Stanwyck plays Lily Powers, whose father has made her serve men in his speakeasy in a Pennsylvania steel town since she was a teenager. After he dies, an old cobbler who reads Nietzsche to her tells her to use men instead of letting them use her. She goes to New York and sleeps her way upward through a bank, department by department, and the camera literally climbs the outside of the building as she rises. New York's state censors demanded changes before the film could be released, Warner Bros. reshot the ending and cut lines, and the softer version was the one most people saw for seventy years. In 2004 a print of the original version was found at the Library of Congress, and it is now the one usually shown.

Jean Harlow, in Red-Headed Woman (1932), written by Anita Loos, plays a secretary who seduces her married boss, breaks up his marriage, and at the end is not punished but riding happily in a car with a new rich man and his chauffeur. Marlene Dietrich, working with Josef von Sternberg at Paramount, played singers and adventuresses who controlled their own desire: in Morocco (1930) she wears a man's tuxedo and kisses a woman in the audience, and in Shanghai Express (1932) she plays a famous courtesan who says, 'It took more than one man to change my name to Shanghai Lily.'

Mae West was something else. She had already been jailed in 1927 for her Broadway play Sex, sentenced to ten days and released after eight. In Hollywood she wrote most of her own dialogue. She Done Him Wrong (1933), adapted from her play Diamond Lil, and I'm No Angel (1933), both with Cary Grant, were among Paramount's biggest hits at a time when the studio was in receivership. West's characters are never punished for liking men; they are in charge of every scene. She was also one of the main reasons Catholic campaigners believed the Code had to be enforced.

Behind the camera, women had less room than in the silent era, but they were there. Dorothy Arzner was the only woman directing features in Hollywood through most of the 1930s. Her pre-Code films include Working Girls (1931), Merrily We Go to Hell (1932), about a woman married to an alcoholic, and Christopher Strong (1933), with Katharine Hepburn as an aviator who must choose between her work and a married lover. Feminist critics in the 1970s, such as Claire Johnston and Pam Cook, returned to Arzner's films to show how a woman could work inside the studio system and still question it, which connects this lesson to the one on feminist film theory. Screenwriters such as Frances Marion, who won Academy Awards for The Big House (1930) and The Champ (1931), and Anita Loos also wrote many of the period's films.

It is important not to romanticise these films. Many of them still end with the bold woman punished, married or dead, and the freedom they show is mostly for white women; Black actors were nearly always servants, and Chinese characters were usually played by white actors in makeup. Anna May Wong, the leading Chinese American actress, plays a courtesan beside Dietrich in Shanghai Express and has one of its strongest roles, but she was repeatedly passed over for leading Chinese parts that went to white actors. The pre-Code era was freer, not fair.

sections.title: Gangsters, chain gangs and forgotten men

blocks.text: The gangster film was the other great pre-Code genre. Prohibition, which lasted from 1920 to 1933, had made bootleggers rich and famous, and newspapers covered Al Capone like a celebrity. In Little Caesar (1931), Edward G. Robinson plays Rico, a small-time hood who rises and falls; his last line is 'Mother of mercy, is this the end of Rico?' In The Public Enemy (1931), directed by William Wellman, James Cagney pushes half a grapefruit into Mae Clarke's face at breakfast, a scene that became famous because it was so casually cruel. Scarface (1932), produced by Howard Hughes and directed by Howard Hawks, with Paul Muni as a character based on Capone, was so violent that censors held up its release for about a year; the studio added the subtitle 'The Shame of the Nation', a prologue condemning gangsters, and an alternative ending.

Warner Bros. also made social problem films. I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang (1932), directed by Mervyn LeRoy and based on Robert Elliott Burns's account of his own escape from a Georgia chain gang, follows a First World War veteran who is unjustly convicted, brutally treated, and escapes twice. In the last scene his girlfriend asks how he lives. He answers from the darkness, 'I steal', and disappears. Heroes for Sale and Wild Boys of the Road (both 1933, both directed by Wellman) followed veterans and teenagers riding freight trains in search of work.

Even the musicals carried the Depression. In Gold Diggers of 1933, Busby Berkeley's last number, 'Remember My Forgotten Man', shows soldiers marching off to war and coming back to bread lines, with Joan Blondell singing for the veterans the country had abandoned. 42nd Street (1933) is about a Broadway show put together by people desperate for work. Berkeley's overhead shots of dozens of chorus girls forming patterns are also, of course, a festival of legs, which is part of why the Code's supporters disliked them.

sections.title: 1933 to 1934: the Legion of Decency and Joseph Breen

blocks.text: By 1933 pressure was building from several directions. The Payne Fund Studies, a group of social science studies of how films affected children, were published that year, and a popular summary by Henry James Forman, Our Movie Made Children, presented them as proof that films taught crime and sex. Women's clubs, Protestant groups and newspapers complained about Mae West and gangster films. But the decisive force was the Catholic Church.

In October 1933 the Apostolic Delegate to the United States, Amleto Giovanni Cicognani, called on American Catholics, in a speech in New York, to unite against what he called the growing immorality of films. The American bishops formed the Legion of Decency, which asked Catholics to sign a pledge to stay away from immoral films; millions did. In June 1934 Cardinal Dennis Dougherty of Philadelphia told Catholics in his diocese to boycott all films. Studios that were already in financial trouble could not afford to lose a large part of their audience in big cities.

The studios gave in. In June 1934 the MPPDA created the Production Code Administration (PCA), headed by Joseph Breen, a Catholic journalist and publicist who had worked on the Code's enforcement since 1933. From July 1934 every film made or distributed by member companies needed a PCA certificate, and a company that released a film without one faced a $25,000 fine. Because the big studios also owned most of the important cinemas, a film without a seal had almost nowhere to play. Breen read scripts before shooting, demanded changes, and checked the finished films. The Code that had existed since 1930 was now enforced.

The effects were immediate. Married couples in films were now usually shown sleeping in separate twin beds. Mae West's films were rewritten until her jokes lost their edge. Tarzan and His Mate (1934) lost its underwater swimming scene with Maureen O'Sullivan's stand-in nude. Some earlier films were refused approval for reissue; Trouble in Paradise was not approved in 1935 and was not seen again until 1968. Betty Boop, the Fleischer studio's flirtatious cartoon character, got longer skirts and became a more homely career girl. Stories about adultery or crime now needed what Breen called 'compensating moral values': the sinner must suffer, the criminal must be caught.

The Code did not stop Hollywood from making films about sex, crime and ambition. It changed how they had to be told: indirectly, with a punishment at the end. Film noir and screwball comedy both grew up under those rules, and many critics think the restrictions made writers cleverer. Others see mainly the loss: women's desire and anger, gay characters and honest stories about race disappeared or went underground for decades. Which side do you find more convincing? Think of a modern rule about what can be shown, such as platform content rules or advertising codes you work with. Does it make creative work sharper, or does it mostly make it narrower?

sections.title: What was happening in Shanghai, Berlin, Tokyo and Taipei

blocks.text: Shanghai in the early 1930s had its own golden age of cinema, centred on the Lianhua and Mingxing studios and a left-wing film movement that made films about workers, poverty and women's lives. The Nationalist government also had a censorship board, which banned films it considered politically dangerous or superstitious. Ruan Lingyu, the biggest star of Chinese silent film, played a mother who sells sex to pay for her son's education in The Goddess (1934), directed by Wu Yonggang, and a writer pushed to suicide by gossip in Cai Chusheng's New Women (1935). The tabloids then attacked her private life, and Ruan killed herself on 8 March 1935, International Women's Day, at the age of twenty-four. So in the same years when Hollywood was punishing its bold women on screen, Shanghai cinema was showing women as victims of a cruel society, and the press destroyed its greatest actress. The Shanghai modernism lesson on Eileen Chang covers the same city a few years later.

In Germany, the last years of the Weimar Republic produced Fritz Lang's M (1931), about a child murderer hunted by the police and the criminal underworld, and Leontine Sagan's Mädchen in Uniform (1931), a story of love between a schoolgirl and a teacher with an almost entirely female cast. After the Nazis took power in January 1933, Joseph Goebbels's ministry set up the Reich Film Chamber, Jewish filmmakers were pushed out, and many, including Lang, left for Hollywood, where some of them later helped create film noir. In the Soviet Union, socialist realism became the official doctrine in 1934, the same year as Hollywood's crackdown.

In Japan, the early 1930s were the last years of silent film, with narrators called benshi still performing live beside the screen. Yasujirō Ozu made I Was Born, But... (1932), a gentle comedy about two boys who are ashamed that their father bows to his boss, and Kenji Mizoguchi was beginning his long series of films about women's suffering. In Taiwan under Japanese rule, films were also shown with live narrators, called 辯士 in Chinese. When the Shanghai film 桃花泣血記 (Peach Blossom Weeps Tears of Blood, 1931), starring Ruan Lingyu, opened in Taiwan in 1932, a promotional song with the same name, written by 詹天馬 and 王雲峰, became one of the first popular Taiwanese-language hit songs. Hollywood, Shanghai and Taipei were connected through the same films and stars.

sections.title: Thirty-four years of the Code, and its return to view

blocks.text: The enforced Code lasted much longer than the pre-Code years it replaced. Will Hays retired in 1945 and Joseph Breen in 1954. Two changes weakened the system. In 1948 the Supreme Court's Paramount decision forced the studios to sell their cinema chains, so a film without a seal could again find screens. In 1952 the Court ruled in Joseph Burstyn, Inc. v. Wilson, a case about Roberto Rossellini's The Miracle, that films were protected by the First Amendment after all, reversing the 1915 decision. Otto Preminger released The Moon Is Blue (1953) and The Man with the Golden Arm (1955) without seals, and Billy Wilder's Some Like It Hot (1959) was also released without one. All three made money.

The Code was rewritten in 1966, and on 1 November 1968 the Motion Picture Association of America replaced it with a ratings system. That opened the door to the New Hollywood of the late 1960s and 1970s, which is covered in its own lesson.

The phrase 'pre-Code' became common only much later, when television showings, repertory cinemas and, in the 1990s and 2000s, home-video collections such as Turner Classic Movies' Forbidden Hollywood series rediscovered the films. Thomas Doherty's 1999 book Pre-Code Hollywood and Mick LaSalle's Complicated Women made the case that this short period was one of the most honest in American film about sex, money and power. For a viewer today, the best way in is simple: watch Baby Face, Night Nurse and She Done Him Wrong, then watch a 1940s film with the same kind of heroine, and notice what the second one is no longer allowed to say.
